title: The spelled-out intro to language modeling: building makemore
note: SYNTHETIC SAMPLE: paraphrased summary of themes from this video, written for offline testing. NOT a verbatim transcript. Run `./run.sh ingest <playlist>` locally to fetch the real one.

segments.text: In this lecture we build makemore, a character level language model, starting from the dumbest baseline: a bigram counting model.
Always start with a simple baseline. A bigram model takes five minutes and gives you a number to beat.
Become one with the data. Before any modeling, look at the examples, print them, count them, check the distribution.
Look at your data with your own eyes; most bugs and most wins come from understanding the dataset.
Evaluate with a single clear metric, here the negative log likelihood, so you know immediately whether a change helped.
Split your data into train, validation and test, and never tune on the test set.
Sample from the model often. Qualitative samples tell you things that the loss number hides.
When the loss is suspiciously good, be suspicious; you are probably leaking information or have a bug.
Add smoothing to the counts so that you never take the log of zero; infinite loss is a classic bug to watch for.
Then we move to a neural network version and verify it reaches roughly the same loss as the counting baseline; that is a sanity check.
Vectorize with tensors and broadcasting, but be very careful: broadcasting bugs are silent and they will bite you.
Check shapes constantly. Print the shape of every tensor when you are unsure; shape mismatches are the most common error.
Scope ruthlessly: get the end-to-end pipeline working with the simplest model, then improve one component at a time.
Under time pressure I would rather have a small model that clearly works and demos well than a big ambitious one that is broken.
Use a pretrained or simple model when you can; you do not need to train from scratch to show the idea.
Keep a log of experiments and what changed; otherwise you forget which tweak actually helped.
Do: start simple, verify every step, visualize, overfit a batch. Don't: add complexity before you have a baseline.
Don't trust code you have not tested on a tiny input where you know the right answer.
